en: The ritual method for painting the image of the Dragon King Kūlika (translated in the Tang as Zunchi) is as follows:
his form is like that of a serpent, manifesting the power of thunder and lightning. His body is golden in color and bound with wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*).
From him arise the flames of *samādhi* as he stands in a posture of trampling with his four feet. Upon his back, seven sharp vajra needles are bristling upward.
A single branch of jade-like horn grows from his forehead;
it encircles the sword upon which the letter *A* is inscribed,
while the visualization of the mind is simultaneously applied, each detail clearly manifest.
If one visualizes him in human form,
his face displays expressions of joy and anger,
and his entire body is covered in armor, like King Vairocana.
The left hand rests upon the waist grasping a rope;
the right arm is bent at the elbow with the palm facing upward, holding a sword;
atop the head sits a coiled dragon king.
He stands upon Vajraparvata.
An alternative version states:
"The Nāga King Kali has the joyful and serene countenance of a deva."
Above his head, seven-headed dragons are depicted;
kneeling on their hams, they gaze upward at the Tathāgata,
joined together in offering a precious lotus flower.
The letter A transforms into this Dragon Messenger;
this letter is a weighty seed of Bodhi.
All who maintain this recitation possess this mind,
for they aspire to unsurpassed bodhi.
Observe these characters upon the sword;
from them all phenomena arise.
This is none other than the bodhicitta.
The dot of practice (*bindu*) signifies the accomplishment of merit and wisdom;
the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) signifies the attainment of *bodhi*;
and the dot of *nirvāṇa* signifies the sense of elimination.
All defilements enter into nirvana.
The repetition of the word is like a great nāga king who possesses great majestic power;
he can raise clouds and bring forth rain with complete mastery.
The letter A is likewise so;
all the deeds of the Tathāgata are born from this letter.
Next is the Dharani-mantra of the Dragon King’s Dharmakāya-mudrā: join the left ring finger and little finger [with the right].
Interlace the palms;
extend the two middle fingers straight upward so they support each other,
and place the two index fingers against the second joints on the backs of the middle fingers.
With both thumbs slightly bent, each should rest against the tips of the middle joints of the two index fingers, moving back and forth;
the position of the elbows is as shown below. The mantra is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ bhuḥ bhūhe bhugapati hūṃ svāhā.* (The first syllable is *oṃ*; the second is *bhuḥ*; the third is *bhūhe*; the fourth is *bhugapati*; the fifth is *hūṃ*; the sixth is *svāhā* with an upa-dhmānīya. This is the Dharma-body seal (*dharmakāya-mudrā*) of all Dragon Kings. Form it by placing the tip of the right hand’s little finger inside the left hand.
With the right hand, slightly bend the fourth finger (ring finger) and place the thumb across the tip of the index finger, also slightly bent;
turn the left hand over and place it upon the right hand.
It is likewise.
With the two hands facing each other in the shape of a snake's mouth,
one should open the four fingers of both hands and move them back and forth.
The mantra is as before.
Next is the Flower Seat Mudrā: the eight fingers of both hands are held slightly curved yet not bent, all pointing upward and held erect.
The two little fingers are two inches apart;
the two middle fingers are each two inches apart from one another;
and the two index fingers are four inches apart.
With the thumbs extended upward and the other two fingers joined together.
Next, the Tooth Seal (*dantamudrā*): bend the right elbow upward.
Bend the ring finger and little finger into the palm;
extend the middle finger straight upward;
and bend the tip of the index finger so that it touches the side of the middle finger joint.
Press the side of the index finger with the thumb.
When performing altar offerings at the prescribed times,
form this mudrā and recite the mantra.
By using the aforementioned [mantra] to summon [the deity] into the center of the altar,
one will immediately cause all to rejoice.
If one wishes to pray for rain, one should duly construct an altar.
By making offerings, one immediately obtains rain in amounts of three, five, seven, eight, nine, one, or two inches, and so forth; the ritual details for this are found in other texts.
Next, the root mantra is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ kugaye karajomigaśanaye svāhā*. Use the aforementioned mudrā. If there is a person suffering from illness:
One should perform the empowerment by binding the mudrā of the Nāga King; then,
while holding a sword and directing the mind toward the highest state,
one should visualize the syllable *A* transforming into a golden dragon.
With a wrathful and radiant appearance,
he causes the patient who contemplates him to be immediately healed.
Whether there be possession by a *graha* spirit, a *bhūta*, or the seizing of a *yakṣa* causing an epidemic.
Located in the southern direction,
for matters concerning malarial fevers and various forms of suffering and affliction,
one should construct a water maṇḍala measuring one cubit.
Place vases at the four corners with fresh flowers inserted into their mouths and adorned with colored blossoms;
alternatively, one may place four vessels in the four directions filled with scented water.
All various articles for offering should be arranged and displayed in a magnificent manner.
He then exhorted the Naga King to remain stationed upon the mandala.
Having placed a sword in the center of the mandala, he set forth the purpose of the rite,
performed prostrations and offerings, and recited the mantra.
Perform the empowerment one hundred and eight times.
Holding a blade, empower the patient;
they will immediately be cured. Then, recite the mantra for dismantling the maṇḍala to dispatch [the deity].
Next, one contemplates the wind-circle shattering the altar;
it is utterly impossible to cause it to remain for long.
This is the secret among secrets of the Dharma.
Do not transmit this arbitrarily.
Kūlika is the king among all nāgas.
The Mañjuśrī-dharmaparyāya and other texts,
including the image-rites of the Naga King Kūlika.
